result.summary: Pausanias describes how Ptolemy Philadelphus married his sister Arsinoe and killed his plotting brothers. He then recounts the revolt of his half-brother Magas of Cyrene, the destruction of the Galati mercenaries, and Ptolemy's defence against Antiochus.

scenes.title: Ptolemy's marriage and brothers
scenes.summary: Ptolemy marries his sister Arsinoe, kills his brother Argæus, brings Alexander's body from Memphis, and kills another brother over Cyprus.
scenes.stakes: Ptolemy's hold on his throne against plotting brothers.

scenes.title: Magas revolts; Galati destroyed
scenes.summary: Magas turns Cyrene against Ptolemy and marches on Egypt but turns back when the Marmaridæ revolt. Ptolemy strands his plotting Galati mercenaries on a desert island of the Nile, where they die.
scenes.stakes: Egypt's safety from invasion and from treacherous mercenaries.

scenes.title: Antiochus checked; Ptolemy's heirs
scenes.summary: Magas urges Antiochus to invade Egypt, but Ptolemy's raiders and army stop him. Pausanias notes Ptolemy's sons were by Lysimachus' daughter, and Arsinoe died childless.

notable_quotes.reason: Notes Ptolemy's sibling marriage, un-Macedonian but Egyptian custom.

analysis.text: The passage shows dynastic violence and suspicion among Alexander's successors, where brothers and allies are constant threats.
Sibling marriage reflects Egyptian royal custom adopted by the Ptolemies, a sign of Hellenistic rulers blending local traditions with Macedonian ones.

fun_facts.text: The Arsinoite district (the Fayum) was named after Arsinoe, as Pausanias notes.

language_notes.text: "Sister on both sides" means full sister, sharing both father and mother, unlike a half-sister.
"Observing that" means he noticed or discovered that his brother was trying to stir revolt in Cyprus.
"Uterine brother" means half-brother through the same mother, here Berenice, but with a different father.
Nomads are wandering herding peoples without fixed towns; the Marmaridæ lived in the desert west of Egypt.
Galati are Gauls (Celts), who often served as mercenaries in Hellenistic armies.
"Guerilla troops" are light raiding forces; the translator uses a modern term for irregular raiders.

context_notes.text: Alexander's body was first taken toward Macedon but diverted to Egypt; Memphis was an old Egyptian capital, and it was later placed in Alexandria.
Cyrene was a Greek city in Libya, which Magas governed and later ruled as king.
The Arsinoite nome (district) is the Fayum region of Egypt, renamed in honor of Arsinoe.

literary_notes.text: The marriage shows Ptolemy adopting Egyptian custom over Macedonian norms, hinting at his political adaptability.
The mercenaries brought to defend Egypt are left to destroy themselves, a grim reversal of their plan to seize it.
Pausanias closes with a flat, matter-of-fact correction, typical of his antiquarian tone.
